Alright students, time for some more quick questions to test your understanding of Control and Coordination! Let's dive in. First question: The growth of pollen tubes towards ovules is an example of which tropism? Is it Hydrotropism, Geotropism, Chemotropism, or Phototropism? Think carefully about the chemical signals involved. The correct answer is (c) Chemotropism. Pollen tubes grow in response to chemical stimuli from the ovule. Next question: How do the shoot and roots of a plant respond to the pull of Earth's gravity? Consider their typical growth directions. Roots grow downwards, towards gravity, exhibiting positive geotropism. Shoots usually grow upwards and away from the Earth, showing negative geotropism. Moving on, can you explain the cause of shoots of the plant bending towards light? What hormone is involved here? Stems are positively phototropic and bend towards light due to more auxin accumulating on the darker side. This causes greater growth on the darker side, bending the stem towards the light source. And finally, define positive geotropism and negative geotropism. Give one example of each. Geotropism is the movement of a plant part in response to gravity. Roots show positive geotropism by growing towards gravity. Stems show negative geotropism by growing away from gravity. Great job, everyone! Keep up the excellent work!

Welcome back, students! Let's test your understanding further with some more questions on Control and Coordination. Ready for the challenge? Our first question is: How do auxins promote the growth of a tendril around a support? Describe in brief. Think about how auxins influence cell growth. The answer is: Auxins produced in the shoot tip move downwards. These auxins cause cell elongation. In tendrils, auxins move away from the contact point with the support, causing more growth on the side away from the support. This unequal growth makes the tendril coil. Next, illustrate with the help of a diagram, the effect of auxins in different parts of a plant. Consider where auxins are formed and their role in various plant parts. The answer to this is: Auxin is formed in the apical meristem of the root and shoot. In the shoot, auxin promotes cell enlargement and inhibits lateral buds, while in the root, it promotes cell division. Now, list in tabular form three differences in the movement of leaves of a Touch-me-not plant when touched and movement of a tendril towards a support. Focus on growth dependence, speed, and direction. Here's the comparison: Mimosa leaves show a growth-independent, fast, and non-directional response. A tendril, however, exhibits a growth-dependent, slow, and directional movement. Our final question for this section: (a) Write the names and one function of each of any three growth hormones in plants. (b) In the absence of muscle cells, how do plant cells show movement? Think about plant hormones and their roles, and how plants respond to stimuli without muscles. For part (a), the three growth hormones are Auxin, which promotes cell elongation and division; Gibberellins, which help in stem growth; and Cytokinins, which promote cell division and delay leaf ageing. For part (b), plants use electrical and chemical means to convey information. For example, Mimosa pudica leaves fold due to turgor changes, which is a growth-independent movement, while directional movements like a seedling breaking through soil are growth-dependent. Great job, everyone! Keep up the excellent work.

Alright students, time for another quick quiz to test your understanding of Control and Coordination! Let's see how well you've grasped these concepts. Ready for your first question? Match the items in Column A with their correct counterparts in Column B. Take a moment to think about each pair. The correct answer is: (i) Reflex action - (e) Sudden response, (ii) Stress hormone - (c) Abscisic acid, (iii) Cytokinin - (d) Cell division, (iv) Hind brain - (b) Vomiting, (v) Fore brain - (a) Thinking. Moving on to the next question. Can you name the two components of the peripheral nervous system? Think about where these nerves originate. The two components are: Cranial nerves arising from the brain and the spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord. Excellent! Now, how does our body maintain its blood sugar level? This involves a crucial feedback mechanism. Our body maintains blood sugar levels through feedback mechanisms. If blood sugar rises, pancreatic cells secrete more insulin, causing the sugar level to fall. Finally, for our last question: First, what is a reflex action? And second, give an example of an involuntary action. A reflex action is an unconscious and involuntary response of effectors to a stimulus. An example of an involuntary action is the beating of the heart or salivation when chewing tasty food. Great job, everyone! You've successfully completed this quiz. Keep reviewing these important concepts!

Welcome back, students! It's time for another round of questions to test your understanding of Control and Coordination. Let's see how well you've grasped the concepts. First question: During exercise, the breathing rate is automatically enhanced. What is the reason behind it? Think about what your body needs when you're active. The answer is: During exercise, the body demands more energy and oxygen. To fulfill these demands, the breathing rate is automatically enhanced, and the heart beats faster, sending a greater volume of oxygenated blood to the muscles. Next up, a drawing challenge! Draw a neat diagram of the human brain and label the Mid brain, Pituitary gland, Cerebellum, and Cerebrum. Or, alternatively, identify the main thinking part of the brain. Take your time to recall the different parts. The answer is: The main thinking part of the brain is the Fore-brain. Now, let's move on to hormones. Explain the feedback mechanism to regulate the action of hormones with the help of one suitable example. Consider how the body maintains balance. The answer is: Hormones should be secreted in precise quantities. The timing and amount of hormone released are regulated by a feedback mechanism. For example, if the sugar level in blood rises, it's detected by the cells of the pancreas, which respond by producing more insulin. As the blood sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced. Finally, state three common features of the respiratory organs of animals. What characteristics do they share to facilitate gas exchange? The answer is: First, all respiratory organs have a large surface area to get enough oxygen. Second, they are thin-walled for easy diffusion of gases and substances. And third, they have a rich supply of blood for transporting respiratory gases. Great job, everyone! Keep practicing and reviewing these important concepts.

Welcome back, students! It's time for another quick quiz to test your understanding of control and coordination. Let's dive right in with our first question. What are the three main functions of the nervous system? Think about how it interacts with our environment and body. Take a moment to recall the key roles of this vital system. The three main functions are: collecting information from surroundings, controlling and coordinating muscle movement, and helping to recognize smell, taste, vision, and hearing with sense organs. Next question! Part A asks you to draw the structure of a neuron and label the cell body and axon. Part B asks: Name the part of the neuron where information is acquired, and through which information travels as an electrical impulse. For part B, information is acquired at the dendrite tip and travels as an electrical impulse from the dendrite to the cell body, then along the axon to its end. Moving on! Brain and spinal cord are two vital organs of our body. How is our body designed to protect them? Consider the structures that safeguard these delicate organs. Our body protects the brain inside a bony box called the cranium, with cerebrospinal fluid acting as a shock absorber. The spinal cord is protected by the vertebral column, or backbone. Here's our final question for this quiz. First, define a receptor and state its location in our body. Mention any two receptors present in our forebrain and their functions. Secondly, how do nerve impulses travel in our body? A receptor is a specialized tip of a nerve cell that receives information from the surroundings, located in sense organs. In the forebrain, gustatory receptors detect taste, and olfactory receptors detect smell. Nerve impulses travel as an electrical impulse created by a chemical reaction at the dendrite tip, moving to the cell body, along the axon, and then releasing chemicals across synapses. Great job, everyone! You've successfully navigated through some challenging questions about control and coordination. Keep up the excellent work!

Welcome back, students! It's time to test your knowledge further with some more challenging questions on Control and Coordination. Let's dive right in! First question: Write names of hormones secreted by the pituitary gland and adrenal gland. State their functions in the body. Also, explain the feedback mechanism for regulation of hormonal secretion with the help of one example. Take a moment to think about this comprehensive question. And here's the answer: The pituitary gland secretes growth hormone, which regulates growth and development. The adrenal gland secretes adrenaline, which creates stress responses. The feedback mechanism, like insulin regulation for blood sugar, ensures precise hormonal control. Moving on to our next question: What happens at the synapse between two neurons? Think about the communication between nerve cells. The answer is: At a synapse, the electrical impulse from one neuron's dendrites is converted into chemical signals by its axon ending, which then transmit to the dendrite of the next neuron. Next up: Design an experiment to demonstrate hydrotropism. How would you show a plant's response to water? Here's a possible experiment: Grow germinating seedlings with a polythene partition separating moist and dry soil. The roots will initially grow downwards but then bend towards the moist soil, demonstrating hydrotropism. And finally, for this section: Why is the use of iodized salt advisable? Consider the role of iodine in your body. The answer is: Iodine is essential for the production of thyroxine hormone, which regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism, ensuring balanced growth. Great job, everyone! Keep up the excellent work.

Alright students, let's test your understanding further with some more questions on Control and Coordination. Get ready to think and recall what we've learned! First question: Why are some patients of diabetes treated by giving injections of insulin? Take a moment to consider the role of insulin. The answer is: Insulin regulates the sugar level in the blood. When this hormone is not synthesised in proper amount, the sugar level in the blood rises, leading to diabetes. That's why diabetic patients receive insulin injections. Moving on to the next one: Which of the following is a plant hormone? Is it Insulin, Thyroxin, Estrogen, or Cytokinin? Think about what we discussed regarding plant growth regulators. The correct answer is (d) Cytokinin. Well done if you got that right! Next up: The gap between two neurons is called a...? Is it a dendrite, a synapse, an axon, or an impulse? Recall the structure of a neuron and how signals are transmitted. The answer is (b) synapse. This is where neurotransmitters play a crucial role. And finally, for our last question: The brain is responsible for...? Is it (a) thinking, (b) regulating the heart beat, (c) balancing the body, or (d) all of the above? Consider the vast functions of the human brain. The correct option is (d) all of the above. The brain is truly a remarkable organ, controlling so many vital processes. Great job tackling these questions! Keep practicing and reviewing these concepts.

Alright students, time for some more questions to test your understanding of Control and Coordination! Let's dive right in. First question: What is the function of receptors in our body? Think of situations where receptors do not work properly. What problems are likely to arise? Take a moment to think about it. And the answer is: All information from the environment is detected by receptors. When receptors do not work properly, information from the environment cannot be detected, and our body cannot respond accordingly. Next up: Draw the structure of a neuron and explain its function. This one requires a bit of drawing and explanation. Here's a breakdown of its function: The information is acquired at the end of the dendrite tip of a nerve cell. The information travels as an electrical impulse from the dendrite to the cell body and then along the axon to its end. Moving on to plants: How does phototropism occur in plants? Consider the chemical compounds involved. The chemical compounds released by stimulated cells for control and coordination in plants are called plant hormones or phytohormones. Auxin controls growth, Gibberellins help in stem growth, Cytokinin promotes cell division, and Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves. Last question for this round: Which signals will get disrupted in case of a spinal cord injury? Think about the different types of actions the spinal cord controls. In case of a spinal cord injury, signals for reflex action and involuntary action will get disrupted. Reflex actions are monitored and controlled through the spinal cord, and signals coming from nerves as well as signals coming to receptors will be disrupted. Great job, everyone! Keep practicing and reviewing these concepts.

Alright students, it's quiz time again! Let's test your understanding of control and coordination with some more challenging questions. Are you ready? First question: How does chemical coordination occur in plants? Think about the specific substances involved. The answer is: Chemical coordination occurs in plants with the help of plant hormones. Next up: What is the need for a system of control and coordination in an organism? Why is it so crucial for survival? The answer to that is: It is necessary that various organs of the body of an organism work together in a proper manner to produce a proper reaction to a stimulus. Moving on to the third question: How are involuntary actions and reflex actions different from each other? Consider their control mechanisms. Here's the difference: Involuntary actions do not require thinking and are controlled by the brain, like a heartbeat. Reflex actions are rapid, spontaneous responses to a stimulus, and do not directly involve the brain. And for our final question in this round: Compare and contrast nervous and hormonal mechanisms for control and coordination in animals. Think about how information is conveyed, its speed, and duration of effects. Let's look at the comparison. In the nervous system, information is conveyed as electric impulses via axons and dendrites, it's rapid, and effects are short-lived. In the hormonal system, information is conveyed as chemical messengers through blood, it's slow, and has prolonged effects. Great job, everyone! Keep up the excellent work.

Welcome back, young scientists! It's time for another quick quiz to test your understanding of Control and Coordination. Let's see how well you've grasped the concepts. Are you ready for the challenge? Great! Let's dive into our first question. What is the difference between the manner in which movement takes place in a sensitive plant and the movement in our legs? Think about the mechanisms involved in each. Take a moment to recall what you've learned about plant responses and animal actions. Here's the answer: A sensitive plant, in response to touch, shows quick movement of leaves which fold up and droop. This is a nastic movement, not growth-related. On the other hand, movement in legs is voluntary. It's an action which is controlled by the cerebellum part of the hindbrain, allowing for conscious control and coordination. Excellent work, everyone! Keep up the great effort. We'll be back with more exciting questions in our next quiz session. Until then, keep exploring the wonders of biology!

Question: The growth of pollen tubes towards ovules is the example of:
(a) Hydrotropism
(b) Geotropism
(c) Chemotropism
(d) Phototropism
Answer: (c) chemotropism
Question: How do the shoot and roots of a plant respond to the pull of earth's gravity?
Answer: Roots grow downwards, towards gravity while shoot usually grow upwards and away from earth.
Question: Explain the cause of shoots of the plant bending towards light.

Answer: Stems are positively phototropic and bend towards the direction of light. The movement is due to occurrence of more auxin on the darker side and lesser auxin on the illuminated side. Thus there is more growth on the darker side which causes the stem to bend towards light.
Question: Define positive geotropism and negative geotropism. Give one example of each.

Answer: The movement of plant part in response to gravity is called geotropic movement and the phenomenon involved is called geotropism. When the tip of the stem grows away from the earth's gravitational forces, it is known as negative geotropism and when the root tips grow towards gravity, it is known as positive geotropism. E.g., Stem shows negative geotropism. Roots show positive geotropism.
Keep learning!

Question: Draw a neat diagram of human brain and label on it the following parts: 1. Mid brain 2. Pituitary gland 3. Cerebellum 4. Cerebrum OR (ii) Which is the main thinking part of brain?
Answer: (ii) Fore-brain. (Optionally show image of human brain with parts labeled)
Question: Explain the feed back mechanism to regulate the action of the hormones with the help of one suitable example.

Answer: Hormones should be secreted in precise quantities. The timing and amount of hormone released are regulated by feedback mechanism. For example, if the sugar level in blood rises, they are detected by the cells of the pancreas which respond by producing more insulin. As the blood sugar level, falls, insulin secretion is reduced.
Question: State three common features of respiratory organs of animals.

Answer: (i) All respiratory organs have large surface area to get enough oxygen. (ii) They are thin-walled for easy diffusion of gases and substances. (iii) They have rich supply of blood for transporting respiratory gases.

Answer:
(i) Collects information from the surroundings.
(ii) Controls and co-ordinates the movement of muscles.
(iii) Helps to recognise smell, taste, vision, hearing etc. with the help of sense organs.

Question:

(b) Name the part of neuron:
(i) Where the information is acquired.
(ii) Through which information travels as an electrical impulse.

Answer (b):
(i) The information is acquired at the end of the dendrite tip of a nerve cell.
(ii) The information travels as an electrical impulse from the dendrite to the cell body and then along the axon to its end.
Question: 'Brain and Spinal cord are two vital organs of our body'. How is our body designed to protect them?

Answer: Brain is located inside a bony box, named as cranium and a fluid is present in this balloon, known as cerebrospinal fluid which is a shock absorber. Spinal cord is placed in a vertebral column and back bone protects it.

Question:
(i) Define receptor and state their location in our body. Mention any two receptors present in our forebrain and their functions.
(ii) How do nerve impulses travel in our body?

Answer (i):
Receptor: Specialised tips of some nerve cells which receive information from the surroundings.
Location: Sense organs
Gustatory receptor: Detect taste
Olfactory receptor: Detect smell

Answer (ii):
The information acquired at the end of the dendritic tip of a nerve cell, sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse, which travels to the cell body, then along the axon to its end, releases some chemicals, across the synapses.

Question: (ii) Explain feedback mechanism for regulation of hormonal secretion with the help of one example.

Question: What happens at the synapse between two neurons?
Answer: At synapse the electrical impulse generated at dendrites of a neuron is passed on to dendrite of another neuron in the form of chemicals by axon ending of the first neuron.
Question: Design an experiment to demonstrate hydrotropism.

Answer: Hydrotropism can be demonstrated with any germinating seedlings, which are allowed to grow on ground. The soil around the roots is separated by a polythene partition. The left side is kept moist and the right side dry. The radicle at first grows in a downward direction and after sometime the roots bend towards the moist soil. This is due to movement of the germinating roots to water.
Question: Why is use of iodised salt advisable?
Answer: Iodine is necessary to make thyroxine hormone which regulates carbohydrates, protein and fat metabolism in the body so as to provide the best balance for growth.

The growth of pollen tubes towards ovules is the example of:
(a) Hydrotropism
(b) Geotropism
(c) Chemotropism
(d) Phototropism
Answer: (c) chemotropism
How do the shoot and roots of a plant respond to the pull of earth's gravity?
Answer: Roots grow downwards, towards gravity while shoot usually grow upwards and away from earth.
Explain the cause of shoots of the plant bending towards light.

Answer: Stems are positively phototropic and bend towards the direction of light. The movement is due to occurrence of more auxin on the darker side and lesser auxin on the illuminated side. Thus there is more growth on the darker side which causes the stem to bend towards light.
Define positive geotropism and negative geotropism. Give one example of each.

Answer: The movement of plant part in response to gravity is called geotropic movement and the phenomenon involved is called geotropism. When the tip of the stem grows away from the earth's gravitational forces, it is known as negative geotropism and when the root tips grow towards gravity, it is known as positive geotropism. E.g., Stem shows negative geotropism. Roots show positive geotropism.

Q: How do auxins promote the growth of a tendril around a support? Describe in brief.

A: Auxins produced in the shoot tip move downwards. These auxins cause cell elongation. In the tendrils, auxins move away from the point of contact with the supporting object. More growth occurs on the side away from the support. As a result of unequal growth on the two sides, the tendril coils around the support.
Q: Illustrate with the help of a diagram, the effect of auxins in different parts of a plant.
A: Auxin is formed in the apical meristem of the root and shoot. In the shoot, auxin promotes cell enlargement and inhibits the development of lateral buds. In the root, auxin promotes cell division.
Q: List in tabular form three differences in the movement of leaves of a Touch-me-not plant (the plant of Mimosa family) when touched and movement of a tendril towards a support.

A:
| S.No | Mimosa Leaves | Tendril |
|---|---|---|
| (i) | Growth independent response | Growth dependent response |
| (ii) | It is a fast process | It is a slow process |
| (iii) | It is non-directional | It is directional |

Q: (a) Write the names and one function of each of any three growth hormones in plants.
(b) In the absence of muscle cells, how do plant cells show movement?

A (a): Three growth hormones in plants are-
(i) Auxin: It promotes elongation and division of cell and root formation.
(ii) Gibberellins: They help in the growth of the stem.
(iii) Cytokinins: They promote cell division and delay leaf ageing.

A (b): Plants use electrical and chemical means to convey information. The leaves of Mimosa pudica fold up in response to touch (growth-independent). Directional movement of a seedling breaking through soil is growth-dependent.
